en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk (Kosiyavagga) 16.
The Training Rule on Wool (Eḷakalomasikkhāpada).
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, while a certain bhikkhu was traveling from the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī, sheep’s wool accrued to him along the way.
Then that bhikkhu tied those sheep’s wool into a bundle with his upper robe and continued on his journey.
When people saw that bhikkhu, they mocked him:
“For how much were they bought by you, venerable sir?
What will the profit be?
Being thus mocked by those men, that bhikkhu became dejected.
Then that bhikkhu went to Sāvatthī and shook those sheep’s wool while standing still.
The bhikkhus said to him:
“Friend, why are you shaking these sheep’s wool while standing still?”
“Indeed, friends, it was for the sake of these sheep’s wool that I was ridiculed by people.
“But from how far away, friend, did you bring these sheep’s wool?
“More than three yojanas, friends.”
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can a monk bring back sheep’s wool over more than three yojanas?
Then those monks, having rebuked that monk in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so on].
“Is it true, monk, that you brought back woolen fleece for more than three yojanas?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
"How indeed, foolish man, could you bring more than three *yojanas* of wool?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“If wool for sheep’s fleece should arise for a bhikkhu while he is traveling on a journey, it may be accepted by that bhikkhu if he so desires.
Having accepted it, he may carry it himself for a maximum distance of three leagues, provided there is no one else to carry it.
If he should carry it further than that, even when there is no one else to carry it, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.”
"But for a bhikkhu who has set out on a journey" means for one traveling along a road.
"Wool may arise" means...
They may arise from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or from relatives, or from friends, or as rag-robes, or by means of one’s own wealth.
“By one who desires” means they should be accepted by one who wishes for them.
"Having received them, they may be carried by hand for a maximum distance of three *yojanas*":
this means they may be carried by hand for a distance not exceeding three *yojanas*.
"If there is no one to carry them."
There is no one else who carries [the goods], whether a woman or a man, a householder or one gone forth.
If she should carry it beyond that, even if there is no carrier,
when she exceeds three yojanas, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the first step.
If she steps beyond the second foot, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If, while standing within three yojanas, she causes [the goods] to fall beyond three yojanas, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If she places [the goods] in another person’s vehicle or merchandise without their knowledge and causes them to go beyond three yojanas, they become subject to relinquishment.
They are to be forfeited to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, they are to be forfeited:
…pe…
“Venerable sir, these sheep’s wool of mine, having been carried more than three yojanas, are subject to forfeiture.
I forfeit them to the Saṅgha. … “He should give them,” … etc.
"May he give... ... [as before] ... "I give it to the Venerable One.
If it is more than three yojanas and he perceives it as more than that, and he causes it to be conveyed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If it is more than three yojanas and he is in doubt, yet he carries it beyond, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If it is more than three yojanas and he perceives it as less, yet he carries it beyond, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is less than three yojanas and he perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is less than three yojanas and he is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is less than three yojanas and he perceives it as less, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He carries it for three yojanas,
he carries it for less than three yojanas,
and he carries it for three yojanas and brings it back as well.
Having gone three yojanas with the intention of staying there, he carries it beyond that point;
or he carries it after having received what was not given;
or he carries it after having received what was relinquished.
Causing another to take it away;
finished goods;
one who is insane.
"For the first offender":
the sixth training rule concerning wool, which deals with the hair of a sheep, is finished.
